title: Protect the market: distributed rate limiting
body:
Worked interview • correctness boundary • 45 minutes

Prompt and scope

Exact prompt: “Design a distributed rate limiter for Corner Market. Protect product browsing, merchant writes, and checkout from accidental overload and abusive clients. Explain what happens when the limiter itself fails.” A rate limiter decides whether an operation may proceed within a configured traffic budget. It does not prove that a client is trustworthy, prevent every denial-of-service attack, or reserve inventory.

Ask before drawing

  • What identity is limited? Assume authenticated account plus route class, with a separate coarse anonymous network limit. Shared network addresses must not be the sole identity for logged-in shoppers.
  • What policy? Assume browsing allows 10 requests/second with a burst of 20, merchant mutation allows 2/second with a burst of 5. Checkout has a separate admission budget and transaction safeguards.
  • How strict? Assume small temporary over-admission is acceptable for browsing, but a merchant's contracted quota must not increase merely because servers are added.
  • Where? One region initially; three regions later. Global billing quotas are a separate durable accounting problem.

Goals and estimates

Assume 100,000 daily active shoppers, 200 API requests per active shopper per day, and a peak ten times the daily average. These are interview inputs, not observed production measurements. Traffic is 20,000,000 / 86,400 = 231.48 requests/second on average; use 2,315 requests/second for peak planning. Assume 50,000 concurrently active identity/route keys. At a planning allowance of 200 bytes per key including overhead, state is about 10 MB per copy; measure the actual datastore representation before buying capacity. One atomic decision per request creates about 2,315 datastore operations/second at peak. A tenfold safety scenario is 23,150 decisions/second, not a claim that one node can sustain it.

The proposed service-level objective (SLO), a measurable reliability target, is 99.9% successful limiter decisions monthly with added latency below 5 milliseconds at the 99th percentile inside the region. A percentile says what fraction of observations finish below a threshold. Set an explicit timeout smaller than the caller's remaining deadline. Rejections should be distinguishable from dependency failures, and policy changes should become visible within one minute.

Interface, state, and diagram

Check(subject, route_class, cost=1, policy_version)
  → {allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reason}
HTTP rejection: 429 Too Many Requests; Retry-After in seconds
bucket key: (tenant_id, subject_hash, route_class, policy_version)
value: {tokens_scaled_integer, last_refill_ms}
policy: {rate_per_second, capacity, expires_at}

Never accept tenant identity or the policy version directly from an untrusted header. Authenticate at the gateway and derive the key there. Hashing an identifier reduces accidental exposure but does not automatically make the data anonymous. Keep raw identities out of metrics labels.

[Client]
   | HTTPS request
   v
[Gateway: authenticate + classify route]
   | bounded Check RPC
   v
[Limiter instances] ---- policy refresh ---- [Versioned policy store]
   | atomic bucket update
   v
[Sharded bucket store: one owner per key]
   |
   +-- allowed --> [Market API]
   +-- denied  --> [429 + retry guidance]

Build the smallest correct design

Start with one process and a token bucket. A token represents permission for one unit of work; the bucket refills at rate r up to capacity B. For elapsed seconds dt, compute available = min(B, old_tokens + r × dt). Admit only if available covers cost, then subtract cost. This bounds accepted work over any interval of length t by roughly B + r × t, assuming a correct monotonic elapsed-time calculation. A full browsing bucket admits 20 immediate requests. Request 21 needs 0.1 seconds of refill at 10 tokens/second.

Two gateways independently storing a full bucket would admit 40 immediate requests. Move each identity's state to a shared owner and combine read, refill, decision, and write into one atomic operation: other requests cannot observe a half-completed update. A short Redis script is one implementation option; atomic script execution does not imply durable global consensus. Use integer-scaled tokens to make rounding explicit, clamp negative elapsed time to zero, and cap large elapsed intervals at a full bucket. Prefer time obtained consistently at the state owner; wall-clock jumps still require a documented policy and tests.

Expire idle bucket state only after enough idle time to refill completely. Deleting a partially empty bucket early grants a fresh burst. Include policy version in the key only with a deliberate migration rule: changing versions resets state and can grant another burst. An alternative updates rate and capacity while preserving and clamping existing tokens. Test rollout behavior, not merely steady state.

Deep dives: contention and geography

Hash identity keys across partitions. A hot merchant remains one hot key even after adding partitions. Local token leases can amortize calls: a central owner grants a gateway a bounded number of tokens, which it spends locally. Define the extra admitted work during a failure as at most the total unspent outstanding leases, provided leases cannot be reused after reassignment. Give leases expiry and an owner generation. This spends accuracy to gain availability and latency; do not describe it as exact.

For three regions, choose a home region for strict per-account policy, accepting remote latency and reduced availability during partitions. For browsing, split a global budget into regional allocations whose sum is bounded and rebalance conservatively. Three regions each enforcing the entire nominal global budget triples the allowance. An exact global decision across a partition cannot simultaneously offer uninterrupted independent regional admission; state the business choice rather than hiding it behind a product name.

Failure analysis and alternatives

If the bucket store times out, browsing may use a deliberately smaller local emergency budget, with a metric identifying degraded decisions. This is bounded fail-open behavior: some requests continue without the normal shared decision. Merchant writes can fail closed with a retriable dependency error, subject to the product's tolerance for lost availability. Neither policy should bypass authentication, authorization, or payment correctness. A retry after an uncertain decision might consume two tokens; conservative double charging is acceptable here, but must not become a duplicate checkout charge.

Reject a fixed one-minute counter when smooth overload control matters: 100 requests at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next may pass almost together. A sliding log records every timestamp and offers a precise rolling window but consumes memory proportional to request volume. A sliding counter is a cheaper approximation. Token buckets fit our explicit burst contract; they do not offer a strict “no more than N in every rolling minute” promise.

Track allowed and denied counts, decision latency, store failures, hot partitions, policy age, and emergency mode usage. Alert on saturation and unexpected admission changes, not on every rejection. Set per-tenant fairness and weighted costs so a cheap metadata lookup and expensive export do not share a misleading one-request cost. Protect the limiter's own API and cap key cardinality to prevent attackers manufacturing endless keys.

Evolution and interview close

Begin with a shared regional state owner plus measured failover behavior. Add partitions after measuring load, leases only after quantifying accuracy tolerance, and regional allocation only when geography requires it. Cost includes one decision per call, replication, policy distribution, and operational complexity. Test two concurrent requests for the final token, clock rollback, policy transition, failover with lost recent state, and a single identity producing most traffic.

Practice: a gateway holds a lease of 8 tokens and crashes. What is the safe interpretation?

The central owner already deducted those 8 tokens. Losing unused tokens temporarily under-admits. Reissuing them before proving they cannot still be spent risks over-admission. A restarted gateway must not reuse an old lease generation.

Interviewer follow-ups and answer rubric

Follow-ups: How does a premium tenant get weighted service? Can a successful retry be charged twice? What exact bound is relaxed during regional failure? Strong: names the quota identity, derives burst behavior, makes state transition atomic, and quantifies degraded admission. Weak: says “put Redis at the gateway,” counts separately on every server, or promises exact global quotas and full partition availability without explaining coordination.

Technical reference checked 2026-10-19: Redis scripting documentation confirms scripts execute atomically and block other server activity while running; keep scripts bounded. All sizing, policies, and architecture choices above are fictional design assumptions.

A short spoken walkthrough

Candidate: Is the limit a strict global entitlement or regional abuse protection?
Interviewer: Begin with regional abuse protection.
Candidate: I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.
Interviewer: Can we simply deploy the same bucket in three regions?
Candidate: Only if the contract permits the multiplied allowance. For a strict global budget I would allocate bounded regional rights or coordinate through one owner; the former can strand capacity and the latter adds latency and partition unavailability. I would keep billing quotas in a separate durable accounting path.

This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Run it later: a durable job scheduler
body:
Worked interview • leases and duplicate effects • 45 minutes

Prompt and clarifications

Exact prompt: “Design a durable scheduler for Corner Market. Merchants schedule sale reminders and nightly inventory reports. Jobs must survive crashes, run close to their requested time, retry safely, and support cancellation.” Durable means acknowledged work remains recoverable after the failures covered by the storage contract. Scheduling decides when work becomes eligible; workers perform the actual effects.

  • One-time or recurring? Assume both. Recurrence uses an explicit named timezone and a defined daylight-saving policy; store each generated occurrence separately.
  • Timing precision? Assume 99% of eligible jobs start within 30 seconds when dependencies are healthy. This is a start-delay target, not a completion promise.
  • Delivery semantics? Assume jobs may execute more than once. The observable business effect should be deduplicated where possible.
  • Cancellation? Define “start” as the successful atomic claim transition into RUNNING. Cancellation that wins before that claim prevents execution; after the claim it is best effort, even if the worker has not yet called the external provider. An email already accepted by an external provider may be impossible to recall.

Numbers that drive choices

Assume 1,000,000 jobs/day, an average runtime of 2 seconds, and a peak arrival rate ten times average. Average rate is 1,000,000 / 86,400 = 11.57 jobs/second; round peak to 116 jobs/second. Little's Law relates average work in progress to throughput times duration in a stable system: at peak, 116 × 2 = 232 concurrent executions. At a planning utilization of 70%, need about 232 / 0.7 = 332 execution slots. Slots are concurrency capacity, not necessarily machines; CPU-heavy and waiting-heavy jobs require different sizing.

At 1 KB of metadata per job and 30 days of retained history, 30 million rows require about 30 GB of raw metadata, before indexes and replication. Large report payloads belong in object storage with references in the job record. If all one million jobs arrive at midnight, the tenfold peak assumption is false: identify scheduled bursts, introduce allowed jitter, and provision or negotiate the completion window.

Other goals: no acknowledged job silently disappears after a single worker failure, tenant isolation, bounded retries, auditable state changes, and a clearly documented disaster recovery point. Recovery point objective is the acceptable amount of recent data loss; recovery time objective is the acceptable restoration duration. Neither follows automatically from “database replication.”

API, state, and architecture

POST /jobs  Idempotency-Key: merchant-scoped-key
{type, payload_ref, run_at_utc, deadline_utc, tenant_id}
GET /jobs/{job_id}
POST /jobs/{job_id}/cancel
jobs(id, tenant_id, type, payload_ref, run_at, state,
     attempt, lease_until, lease_generation, idempotency_key,
     request_hash, last_error, created_at)
UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key)
INDEX(state, run_at, id)
job_events(job_id, sequence, state, reason, occurred_at)

Idempotency means repeating the same logical request has the same intended effect. Reuse of a key with a different request body returns a conflict instead of silently changing the job. Authenticate ownership before reads and cancellations. Permit only registered job types and validated parameters; arbitrary uploaded code is a different, much harder isolation problem.

[Merchant] -- create/cancel --> [Job API]
                                  |
                                  v
                          [Durable job database]
                                  ^
                                  | claim due rows + lease
                          [Worker pool per job class]
                                  |
                      idempotent business operation
                                  v
                      [Report store / delivery provider]

[Lease reaper] --> expired running jobs --> retry eligibility
[Recurrence expander] --> uniquely keyed future occurrences

Progressive design: transaction first

Start with a database-backed queue. Workers select due pending rows inside a short transaction, acquire row locks, and update them to running with a lease. A lease grants temporary ownership until a timestamp. With PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets competing workers skip already locked rows; its inconsistent view is suitable for queue-like selection, not general reporting. Commit the claim before doing slow external work. Holding database locks while generating a report or calling an email service ties storage availability to slow dependencies.

Each claim increments lease_generation. Completion is conditional on matching job ID, running state, and generation. A stale worker whose lease expired cannot overwrite a newer worker's result. This generation is a fencing token, a monotonically increasing ownership marker. It fences database state; an external effect also needs its own deduplication or fencing support. Heartbeats extend leases with the same generation. Pick a lease longer than normal execution and renew well before expiry, while accepting that pauses and network partitions can still cause overlapping workers.

Poll due work every second with a bounded batch. Use the database clock consistently for due and lease comparisons. Add randomized poll delays and an index so idle workers do not repeatedly scan history. Separate short notifications from long reports, and enforce tenant concurrency limits so one merchant cannot occupy every slot. A broker can later transport ready jobs, but the database remains the authority for scheduled eligibility; publishing must then use a transactional outbox to avoid losing jobs between commit and send.

The unavoidable duplicate window

Consider a worker that sends a reminder successfully and crashes before marking the job completed. The lease expires and another worker retries. Marking complete before sending instead creates a lost-effect window. A scheduler alone cannot make an arbitrary external side effect happen exactly once. Pass the stable occurrence ID as the downstream idempotency key when the provider supports a documented durable deduplication contract. Otherwise record the uncertainty and choose explicitly between possible duplicates and possible omission.

For reports, write output under a stable job-derived object key and publish a manifest conditionally. For internal database work, insert the business effect and mark completion in the same transaction when both share a database. A unique constraint on effect ID is the final concurrency defense. Retain deduplication records long enough to cover retries, replays, and backup restoration; a five-minute record is insufficient if operators can replay a month later.

Retries, cancellation, and failure

Classify permanent validation errors separately from temporary timeouts. Retry temporary failures with exponential backoff and random jitter, cap both attempts and elapsed time, and stop after the job deadline. A dead-letter state preserves exhausted work for inspection; it is not an unmonitored trash folder. Alert on oldest eligible age, failure rate by class, lease expiry, and queue depth. Compare incoming work with sustainable completion rate: if arrival exceeds processing, no retry policy can prevent backlog growth.

Cancellation uses a conditional update. Pending becomes cancelled; running becomes cancel_requested, and the worker checks between safe steps. Cancellation and completion racing must have an explicitly allowed outcome. Recurring schedules need a stable occurrence key such as schedule ID plus intended UTC instant, a timezone database version or documented update policy, and a choice for missed runs after outages: catch up all, latest only, or skip. Never “just add 24 hours” to model every local calendar day.

Database failover can repeat claims if recent writes were lost. Ensure the promised recovery point matches business expectations, keep effects idempotent, and test restoration. A worker that loses connectivity must stop starting new effects once it cannot renew ownership; a paused process resuming later still requires fencing. Large outages may create retry storms, so recover gradually with global and tenant admission controls.

Alternatives, evolution, and assessment

Reject an in-memory timer on an API server: restarts erase it, replicas disagree, and deployments shift responsibility. Reject a single cron entry per job at this scale: mutation, cancellation, observability, and ownership become fragile. Begin with indexed due rows; shard by tenant or due-time bucket only when measured lock contention or storage demands it. Partition old history for retention and benchmark due-row queries at realistic backlog sizes. Cost follows retained metadata, polling frequency, execution duration, and repeated work.

Practice: the job takes 90 seconds but its lease is 30 seconds. Diagnose and redesign.

Without renewal, another worker can start at 30 seconds. Renew the lease conditionally, measure heartbeat health, and retain generation checks. This reduces overlaps but does not eliminate them; make effects idempotent. For a non-idempotent external operation, reconcile its status after an uncertain response rather than blindly retrying.

Interviewer follow-ups and rubric

Follow-ups: What happens after a week-long outage? How do you stop a noisy tenant? Can an operator replay a succeeded job? Strong: separates start from completion, calculates concurrency, explains the duplicate window, and shows conditional ownership transitions. Weak: promises exactly-once email, holds locks through network calls, or treats a queue as a complete recurring scheduler.

Technical reference checked 2026-10-19: PostgreSQL SELECT and locking documentation describes SKIP LOCKED and its queue-oriented use. The selected architecture and all workload numbers are exercise assumptions.

A short spoken walkthrough

Candidate: Does no duplicate job mean one accepted owner or one external side effect?
Interviewer: The business wants one reminder email.
Candidate: I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.
Interviewer: A paused worker wakes after its lease expires. Are we safe?
Candidate: The new epoch fences state writes only where the receiver checks it. For email I need provider idempotency on a stable effect ID or must disclose the duplicate-versus-loss tradeoff after an unknown result. I cannot promise one email merely because the queue has one current owner.

This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: The last basket: inventory, reservations, and payments
body:
Worked interview • business invariants • 50 minutes

Exact prompt and business contract

Exact prompt: “Corner Market sells limited bakery pickup boxes. Design reservation and checkout so two shoppers cannot buy the last box, retries do not duplicate a charge, and payment failures do not strand inventory forever.” The central invariant, a rule that must always hold, is that confirmed plus active reserved units never exceed sellable inventory for a stock item. Payment correctness is a second invariant: one order must not accumulate multiple unintended successful charges.

  • Assume each checkout contains stock from one merchant; cross-merchant carts are out of scope for the first version.
  • Assume a reservation lasts five minutes, but payment attempts started before expiry need explicit reconciliation before stock is released.
  • Assume the payment provider supports idempotency keys and status lookup. Its precise key retention and webhook behavior must be checked before implementation.
  • Assume authorization holds funds and capture requests settlement; availability and timing depend on the chosen provider and payment method. We do not build a card network or store card credentials.

Scale and nonfunctional goals

Assume 100,000 daily shoppers and 0.2 checkout attempts per shopper/day: 20,000 attempts/day, or 0.2315/second average. A 100-fold promotion peak gives 23.15 attempts/second overall. This modest aggregate does not remove contention: 2,000 simultaneous requests may target the same final 100 boxes. Model hot-item contention separately from average throughput.

Assume five minutes of active reservations at 23.15/second during a sustained peak: approximately 6,945 active reservations. At 1 KB per reservation, raw active records are roughly 6.95 MB. Twenty thousand orders/day at 2 KB each produce 40 MB/day before indexes, events, and replicas. Transaction contention and correctness dominate this exercise more than storage volume.

Target reservation responses below 300 milliseconds at the 99th percentile in-region, excluding the external payment interaction. Set a proposed 99.9% monthly reservation availability target, but never silently oversell to meet it. During an inventory partition, decline or defer affected reservations. A charge can remain pending when the outcome is unknown; showing “failed” prematurely encourages harmful retries. Maintain an auditable state history and keep sensitive payment data with the provider.

Model and interfaces

POST /reservations  Idempotency-Key: customer-scoped-key
{merchant_id, items:[{sku, quantity}]}
→ {reservation_id, expires_at, total_minor_units, currency}
POST /orders/{id}/pay  Idempotency-Key: payment-attempt-key
GET /orders/{id} → {order_state, payment_state}
stock(merchant_id, sku, sellable, reserved, sold, version)
reservations(id, customer_id, state, expires_at, order_id)
reservation_items(reservation_id, merchant_id, sku, quantity)
orders(id, reservation_id UNIQUE, total_minor_units, currency, state)
payment_attempts(id, order_id, provider_key UNIQUE,
                 provider_reference, state, amount_minor_units)
request_results(customer_id, operation, idempotency_key, request_hash,
                state, response, UNIQUE(customer_id, operation, idempotency_key))
outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, aggregate_id, type, payload, sent_at)

Use integer minor currency units and a currency code; do not calculate money with binary floating point. Obtain prices from trusted server state and store the quoted order amount. Define rounding and tax rules separately. Create or lock the scoped request record in the same transaction as the reservation/order effect. A concurrent identical key waits for the durable result or receives an explicit in-progress response. Lock the order before creating a payment attempt, and enforce at most one live attempt per order (for example a partial unique index over order_id for pending/unknown attempts). A different client key must not bypass that order invariant. Reconcile an unknown attempt before permitting another charge attempt. A request hash prevents one idempotency key being reused with different items. A uniqueness constraint is enforced in storage, not by an earlier “does this exist?” query that races.

[Shopper] --> [Checkout service] --> [Inventory + order database]
                    |                       |
                    | provider key          | transaction includes outbox
                    v                       v
             [Payment provider]       [Outbox publisher]
                    |                       |
                    +-- webhook --> [Reconciler] --> [Order state transition]
                                            |
                                      [Expiry worker]
                               checks payment uncertainty first

Progressive design: keep stock atomic

Begin with one transactional database for a merchant's inventory and orders. A transaction updates stock only if sellable - reserved - sold >= requested_quantity, then inserts the reservation and order. Check affected row count. For several stock items, lock rows in a deterministic SKU order, verify all quantities, and commit all or none. Consistent locking order reduces deadlocks; the application must still retry a deadlock-aborted transaction safely. Do not read availability, release the connection, and later subtract: both buyers could read one remaining unit.

For 100 boxes, reserving 3 sets reserved to 3 and leaves 97 available. Confirmation moves 3 from reserved to sold in one transaction; availability stays 97. Expiry moves 3 out of reserved and leaves sold unchanged. Every transition checks the current reservation state. Expiring twice cannot release 6 units. A cache may show approximate availability for browsing, but the transactional conditional update decides whether checkout succeeds.

A durable state machine makes permitted transitions explicit: HELD → PAYMENT_PENDING → CONFIRMED, or HELD → EXPIRED; PAYMENT_PENDING may become CANCELLED only after the payment outcome is resolved. Persist an attempt before calling the provider. Use its stable key for retries of that same attempt. If the response is lost, query or reconcile the original attempt instead of creating a new key and another possible charge.

Where a transaction stops

The inventory database and external provider do not share our local transaction. Use a saga, a sequence of durable steps with compensating actions when later steps cannot complete. Authorize funds, atomically confirm stock and order if the reservation is still eligible, then capture according to the business contract. If stock confirmation cannot complete after authorization, void the authorization when supported. If capture happens but finalization fails, reconcile and either complete the order or refund. Refund is a new business action that may take time and fail; it does not erase the original charge.

An authorization-first workflow needs a policy for capture failure after confirmation: retain the order in a recoverable pending state, retry within a bounded window, then cancel and release or return stock according to merchant policy. Reserving inventory during payment uncertainty reduces immediate availability but avoids selling the same box to someone else. Describe this tradeoff to the interviewer; there is no magic ordering that eliminates all external uncertainty.

Insert order events into an outbox in the same transaction as the business transition. A publisher sends unsent events and may send twice after a crash; consumers deduplicate using event ID. Publishing directly before commit creates phantom events, while publishing only afterward without durable intent can lose events. Webhooks can also be duplicated or arrive out of order. Authenticate provider signatures, deduplicate provider event IDs, and reconcile against permitted state transitions and authoritative provider status rather than trusting arrival order.

Failures, alternatives, and operating model

An expiry worker conditionally expires only eligible held reservations. It cannot blindly release PAYMENT_PENDING stock at five minutes: a charge might have succeeded during a timeout. Track an uncertainty deadline, look up provider status, and escalate stuck cases with operational visibility. Use the database's time for expiry comparisons. Test the exact boundary where expiry and confirmation race, plus crash-after-provider-success and duplicate-webhook sequences.

Reject a cache lock as the sole overselling defense: lease expiry can let another process enter while the first still runs. Reject separate inventory writes followed by order writes without a transaction or documented compensation. Reject a blanket claim of “exactly-once payments”; the relevant guarantee is stable request identity plus provider deduplication, reconciliation, and constrained state transitions.

Track reserved-age distribution, payment-pending age, stock invariant violations, authorization-to-capture lag, reconciliation backlog, and duplicate-key conflicts. Log correlation IDs and provider references without storing secrets. Restrict refund and manual-adjustment privileges; audit operator actions. Reconcile totals against provider settlement records on a scheduled basis because callbacks alone are not a financial ledger.

Scale by merchant when merchants own disjoint stock. A single hot SKU remains serialized at its correctness boundary; shard counters only with an explicit stock-allocation scheme whose allocations sum to the actual stock. Multi-region writes should route a stock owner to one authoritative region or use an appropriate strongly coordinated store. Cross-region independent decrements cannot safely enforce one remaining unit during a partition. Evolve cross-merchant carts into per-merchant reservations with explicit partial-failure handling, rather than pretending the original single-database transaction extends globally.

Practice: the provider times out, then the shopper presses Pay again. What should the service do?

Return the existing attempt's pending status, retry or look up that attempt using its original provider key, and reconcile. Do not assume timeout means failure. If the provider's deduplication window has elapsed, investigate before issuing another charge.

Follow-ups and rubric

Follow-ups: What if price changes during checkout? Who can adjust stock? What happens when refunds fail? Strong: states invariants, demonstrates conditional updates, exposes payment uncertainty, and names the recovery owner. Weak: reads cached stock as authoritative, uses a new key for every retry, or releases stock while payment status is unknown.

Technical reference checked 2026-10-19: PostgreSQL row-locking documentation. Provider-specific payment guarantees are intentionally requirements to verify, rather than assumed universal behavior. All merchant and workload details are fictional.

A short spoken walkthrough

Candidate: What should happen if payment succeeds after the hold expires?
Interviewer: Do not oversell; refund if stock cannot be obtained safely.
Candidate: I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.
Interviewer: Why not roll back the SQL transaction to reverse the charge?
Candidate: The provider is another authority. A local rollback cannot undo its committed effect. I reconcile the stable payment identity, then attempt the permitted order transition. If inventory cannot be reacquired, I create an auditable refund action with its own retry and reconciliation state, rather than calling the whole workflow atomic.

This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Count what happened: merchant analytics and streaming
body:
Worked interview • time, replay, and accounting boundaries • 45 minutes

Prompt and assumed answers

Exact prompt: “Build Corner Market's merchant dashboard showing product views, checkout conversion, and paid order totals within one minute. Support historical reports and recovery after processing outages.” Streaming means processing a continuing sequence of events incrementally. An event is a record of something that happened, with an identity and occurrence time; it is not automatically a unique or trustworthy fact.

  • Is the dashboard financially authoritative? Assume view and funnel numbers are approximate operational analytics. Paid totals originate from confirmed order transitions and are reconciled against the order database. Settlement reporting is separate.
  • How fresh? Assume 95% of valid events become queryable within 60 seconds during healthy operation. Late events can correct recent windows for 24 hours.
  • How long retained? Assume 7 days in the replay log, 1 year in object storage, and 90 days of fine-grained aggregates.
  • Can clients resend? Yes. Client timestamps may be wrong, and mobile devices can upload later. Trust server-recorded order events more than client claims.

Capacity and contracts

Assume 100,000 daily shoppers, each producing 50 product-interaction events/day. That is 5,000,000 events/day, or 57.87/second average. Tenfold peak is about 579/second. At 500 bytes per encoded event, raw traffic is 2.5 GB/day, 17.5 GB for seven days, or 52.5 GB with three log copies, before protocol overhead and indexes. A year of raw events is approximately 912.5 GB before compression and redundant storage. Compression is workload-dependent; benchmark rather than claiming a universal ratio.

Assume 2,000 merchants, 20 relevant products per merchant, and two event counters per one-minute window. A dense upper bound is 2,000 × 20 × 2 × 1,440 = 115.2 million counter cells/day. Sparse activity, coarser historical windows, and retaining only useful dimensions can save far more than changing storage brands. Do not materialize every user, product, region, campaign, and device combination without a query requirement.

The proposed ingestion target is 99.9% monthly successful server acknowledgments after the configured durable log write. Define which failures that durability covers. Track ingestion latency separately from end-to-end freshness. A service can accept every event while its dashboard is hours stale.

Event contract and architecture

POST /events/batch
{events:[{event_id, event_type, schema_version, occurred_at,
          session_id, product_id, merchant_id}]}
server adds: received_at, authenticated_subject, validation_result
order event: {event_id, order_id, order_version,
              merchant_id, paid_minor_units, currency, occurred_at}
aggregate key: (merchant_id, product_id, window_start,
                metric_name, metric_definition_version)
GET /merchants/{id}/metrics?from=...&to=...&resolution=hour

Use an allowlist of event types, maximum batch size, schema validation, and rate limits. A schema version identifies the shape of data; a metric-definition version identifies the meaning of a computed number. They solve different problems. Server-issued merchant identity prevents one merchant writing or reading another merchant's data. Minimize personal fields and define consent, deletion, and retention requirements before collecting them.

[Web/mobile] --> [Validated ingest] --> [Partitioned durable log]
[Order database + outbox] --------------------^
                                              |
                       +----------------------+------------------+
                       v                                         v
               [Stream processor]                        [Raw object archive]
           dedupe + event-time windows                    replay / batch repair
                       |
                       v
               [Aggregate query store] <-- versioned correction job
                       |
               [Merchant dashboard API]
                       |
              [Reconciliation against orders]

Start simple, then make time explicit

Begin with server-side order events written through the transactional outbox and a batch dashboard refreshed every minute. Add client views through validated ingestion. Partition the log by merchant when ordered merchant processing is useful, but recognize that one large merchant can become a hot partition. Partitioning by merchant plus a stable subkey spreads load at the cost of merging partial aggregates. Log order is normally scoped to a partition; do not assume one global ordering of every shopper's actions.

Distinguish event time, when the action occurred, from processing time, when the processor handled it. A phone records a view at 12:00 but reconnects at 12:10. Counting by processing time puts the view in the wrong minute. Count valid events into event-time windows, with a policy for implausible client timestamps. Use received time or quarantine when timestamps are outside accepted bounds, and disclose this interpretation in metric definitions.

A watermark is the processor's estimate of how far event-time progress has advanced. It is a policy informed by observations, not proof that older events can never arrive. With a two-minute lateness allowance, a window can publish a provisional value promptly, then accept updates. Our contract permits corrections for 24 hours; older arrivals go to a repair path or a separately labeled late-event count. Define what a dashboard displays when a previous total changes.

Duplicates, replay, and the denominator

Deduplicate by stable event ID within an explicit retention window. At 5 million events/day and 24 hours of deduplication, 32 bytes per ID is 160 MB raw before state-store overhead. A duplicated event arriving after that window can be counted again unless archival repair or a longer-lived unique record catches it. Do not sell bounded deduplication as eternal uniqueness.

Make aggregate writes replay-safe. One option writes deterministic window values keyed by window and processor version, replacing prior values rather than blindly incrementing on every delivery. Another commits processed offsets and output in a transactional boundary supported by the chosen stack. Broker-level transactional processing does not make arbitrary external databases, emails, or downstream APIs exactly once. Verify the entire boundary. During repair, write a new version of aggregates and atomically switch readers after validation instead of mixing old and new partial results.

Conversion needs a definition. “Paid orders / views” is not the same as “sessions with a paid order / sessions with a product view.” Suppose 1,000 eligible sessions contain views and 80 of those sessions pay: conversion is 80 / 1,000 = 8%. If those sessions generated 4,000 views, dividing 80 by 4,000 yields 2%, a different metric. Establish attribution window, identity rules, bot treatment, and timezone boundaries before implementing joins. Cross-device identity and missing events limit certainty; display suitable caveats.

Failure and operational decisions

If a processor is down for two hours while traffic averages 58/second, backlog is about 417,600 events. A recovering processor able to handle 300/second while 58/second continue arriving drains at 242/second, requiring about 1,726 seconds, or 28.8 minutes. Simply dividing by 300 understates recovery time. Provision and alert using remaining retention headroom: once seven-day log data expire, recovery needs the object archive.

Poison events must not stall an entire partition forever. Preserve failed events with reason and schema version in a quarantined stream, count them, and provide a controlled replay tool. For a query-store outage, stop or buffer within bounded capacity rather than silently advancing progress and dropping output. Track oldest unprocessed event, source-to-dashboard delay, duplicates, late-event rate, invalid events, state growth, and reconciliation differences.

Reject querying the production order database for every dashboard refresh: analytics scans can impair checkout and cannot reconstruct client views. Reject treating a cache increment as an auditable financial total. Reject starting with a complex stream platform if minute-level batch satisfies requirements. Add streaming when latency, volume, and operational ownership justify it; ongoing cost includes replicas, retained data, state checkpoints, repair jobs, and on-call expertise.

Evolution and practice

Keep immutable source events under retention rules, version transformations, and support deterministic backfills. If regulations require deletion, an append-only slogan does not override it: implement deletion or cryptographic and storage controls appropriate to the requirement, and propagate effects to derived data. Keep order correctness outside the analytics path so a dashboard outage cannot stop checkout.

Practice: a replay doubles paid totals. What failed, and how do you repair it?

The sink probably increments totals without deduplicating event IDs or replacing deterministic windows. Pause publication, rebuild a new aggregate version from trusted order events, compare totals to authoritative orders, and switch readers after validation. Preserve the bad run for audit without exposing it as current data.

Follow-ups and rubric

Follow-ups: What does “one minute” measure? How do definitions change? What happens beyond retention? Strong: distinguishes times, derives backlog recovery, defines denominators, and bounds deduplication. Weak: promises exactly-once end to end from a broker setting, ignores late events, or confuses dashboard totals with settlement accounting.

Technical reference checked 2026-10-19: Apache Kafka design documentation explains partition ordering and the scope of transactional processing guarantees. Workload, lateness, and retention policies above are chosen interview assumptions.

A short spoken walkthrough

Candidate: Are these dashboard counts provisional or financial settlement records?
Interviewer: Provisional product dashboards with later corrections.
Candidate: I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.
Interviewer: A replay sends every event again. Will counts double?
Candidate: Not if identity, retention and aggregate replacement are designed together. I deduplicate stable event IDs within the declared horizon and rebuild into a new version before cutover. Events older than that horizon require a separate controlled backfill. Financial settlement would need stronger source reconciliation and an explicit accounting contract.

This is the compact interview explanation. The earlier sections expand the mechanism and failure traces; adapt the time spent on them to the interviewer’s direction.

title: Elective: reliable AI recommendations and feature serving
body:
Worked interview • data freshness and safe fallback • 45 minutes

Exact prompt and scope

Exact prompt: “Corner Market wants personalized product recommendations. Design the feature and inference serving path, including training consistency, freshness, failure behavior, and safe rollout.” A feature is a measurable input to a model, such as a customer's seven-day category-view count. Inference is applying a trained model to inputs to obtain a prediction. This elective follows analytics because it reuses event collection, replay, and freshness reasoning; it is not a requirement to add artificial intelligence to every system.

  • What outcome? Assume rank up to 200 eligible candidate products and return 20. Candidate generation chooses a smaller relevant set; ranking orders that set.
  • What model? Assume a compact CPU-served ranking model, not a large language model. Model training research and graphics-processor infrastructure are outside this interview's scope.
  • What quality contract? Assume experiments evaluate useful purchases and user experience, with guardrails for errors, latency, stale inventory, and merchant concentration. No guaranteed business uplift is claimed.
  • Which data? Assume consented product interactions and current catalog eligibility. Never use payment credentials or sensitive personal attributes as features.

Capacity, latency, and freshness

Assume 100,000 daily shoppers request 20 recommendation panels/day: 2,000,000 requests/day, or 23.15 requests/second average. Tenfold peak is 232/second after rounding upward. At 200 candidates/request, peak scoring demand is 46,400 candidate scores/second. Benchmark the actual model and batch shape; this arithmetic does not determine how many CPU cores are sufficient.

Assume 20 user features at 8 bytes each for 100,000 users: 16 MB raw numeric values. Forty thousand products with 30 eight-byte features require 9.6 MB raw. Keys, missing-value indicators, timestamps, versions, replicas, serialization, and indexes add overhead. Fetching 200 candidate vectors separately would produce 46,400 remote lookups/second at peak. Batch reads and compact cached item features reduce remote call count; monitor payload size as well as calls.

Set a proposed 99th-percentile response target of 150 milliseconds. A sequential budget might allocate 10 ms gateway/network overhead, 20 ms candidate retrieval, 25 ms feature retrieval, 40 ms inference, 15 ms eligibility filtering and response, plus 40 ms reserve. These sum to 150 ms but do not prove the system's 99th percentile: component tails correlate, network conditions vary, and end-to-end load tests are required. Assume user interaction features should be less than five minutes old, catalog availability less than one minute old, and recommendations may fall back safely if these goals are missed.

Interfaces, contract, and flow

GET /recommendations?context=home&limit=20
→ {items, request_id, model_version, fallback_reason?}
feature definition: {name, type, entity_key, transformation_version,
                     event_time_semantics, freshness_limit, default}
online row: (entity_id, feature_set_version)
  → {values, source_event_time, computed_at, expires_at}
model manifest: {model_version, required_feature_set,
                 schema_hash, artifact_digest, rollout_policy}
exposure event: {request_id, model_version, candidate_ids,
                 displayed_ids, experiment_assignment, occurred_at}

A model manifest declares the required inputs; deployments must reject incompatible feature versions. Do not expose unnecessary user features in the client response. An exposure event records what the user actually saw, so offline evaluation can distinguish unseen candidates from displayed results. Restrict access to feature data and bound retention independently for raw events, derived features, and experiment logs.

[Interaction events] --> [Versioned transformations]
                             |                  |
                             v                  v
                    [Historical feature store] [Online feature store]
                             |                  ^
                    point-in-time training      | materialization
                             v                  |
                      [Model validation] --> [Versioned registry]
                                                  |
[Request] --> [Candidate retrieval] --> [Batch feature lookup]
                                                  |
                                                  v
                                          [Model inference]
                                                  |
                               [Current eligibility filter]
                                                  |
                             [Ranked response / popular fallback]

Progressive design: earn the model

Start with a nonpersonalized baseline: available popular items by neighborhood and category, with explicit merchant and safety rules. It establishes an availability fallback and a measurable comparison. Add offline-trained ranking only when the product question and evaluation data justify it. Keep catalog eligibility authoritative outside the model: a high predicted score never authorizes sale of unavailable stock, bypasses access rules, or overrides a merchant's removal.

Generate candidates using simple category and popularity indexes first. Fetch user features once and item features in a batch; cache shared item vectors with versioned keys. Score the candidate batch within a bounded deadline and filter current eligibility before responding. If fewer than 20 remain, fill from the safe baseline or return fewer, according to the user experience contract. Avoid unlimited retries that exceed the request's deadline.

Feature freshness requires two timestamps. source_event_time indicates the newest source fact incorporated; computed_at indicates processing time. Recomputing from yesterday's input now produces a recent computation timestamp with stale information. Check the appropriate freshness measure per feature. A missing feature and a measured zero are different values: include a missing indicator or a documented training-consistent default, and record how frequently defaults are used.

Training consistency and temporal leakage

Training-serving skew means training and online inference compute inputs differently. A seven-day count calculated in UTC during training and local days online is one example. Share versioned transformation logic where practical, test with fixed event sequences, and compare sampled online feature values with offline recomputation. A shared codebase alone does not guarantee identical data arrival, window boundaries, or missing-value behavior.

Point-in-time correctness means constructing each training row only from information available at that row's prediction time, subject to the system's actual availability contract. If a shopper was scored at 10:00, a purchase at 10:05 must not enter that score's features. Late-arriving historical data can also leak knowledge if a backfill uses facts not available online at 10:00. Keep event time and availability time where the use case needs both. Join features as of the example timestamp and preserve labels separately.

Use time-based evaluation splits when predicting future behavior, avoid users or sessions accidentally leaking between incompatible splits, and compare against the baseline. Offline ranking metrics are proxies; run a controlled experiment with stable assignment and latency/error guardrails before broad release. Statistical methodology belongs in a dedicated experiment lesson, but the architecture must capture assignment, exposure, outcome, and model version so analysis is possible.

Failures and rollout

If the online store fails, use bounded cached features only within their declared freshness window or fall back to popular eligible items. If inference exceeds its deadline, return fallback and count the timeout. Do not silently serve arbitrary default vectors for every user and call the resulting output personalized. Track fallback rate, feature age, missing-feature rate, schema rejection, batch size, inference latency, and output score distributions.

Deploy a model and its compatible feature set together through a manifest. Preload artifacts, validate checksum and schema, warm instances, and route a small fraction of traffic before expansion. Shadow mode computes predictions without changing the displayed result; it helps measure latency and output differences but does not measure actual user response to the shadow output. Canary rollout exposes a small real audience and therefore requires business guardrails. Keep the previous compatible artifact and feature contract for rollback.

A traffic spike can overwhelm feature storage before model CPUs. Apply admission controls, cap candidates, batch reads, and degrade in a measured order. Cache keys containing only user ID can accidentally mix model or feature versions; include the relevant version and context. Limit cache lifetime for personalization, and prevent cross-user cache leakage through authenticated key construction. A feature pipeline outage should not make checkout unavailable: recommendation and purchase correctness have different dependency budgets.

Alternatives, evolution, and interview close

Reject a synchronous full-history warehouse query on every recommendation request: it moves large scans into a tight latency budget. Reject adding a vector database merely because the feature is called AI; ordinary indexed candidate retrieval may satisfy this compact model. Embedding retrieval becomes justified when learned similarity improves candidate quality under measured cost and latency. Reject running a large generative model for this assumed ranking workload without evidence of benefit.

At multi-region scale, replicate relatively stable item features, route user state deliberately, and document freshness during pipeline partitions. Keep model artifacts identical by digest, but allow controlled regional rollouts. Cost includes feature computation, online reads, model execution, experiment logging, retraining, and operational support. Compare benefit with the popular baseline and remove complexity that fails to earn its cost.

Practice: offline accuracy improves dramatically after a backfill, but online results do not. What do you inspect?

Check temporal leakage, availability-time joins, changed metric definitions, selection bias, feature defaults, train/serve transformations, and exposure logging. Reconstruct a historical request using only data actually available then. A larger model is not the first repair.

Follow-ups and rubric

Follow-ups: How do deletion requests propagate? What does a safe fallback show? How do you roll back incompatible inputs? Strong: defines freshness and feature versions, separates eligibility from prediction, identifies leakage, and includes a baseline. Weak: adds a vector database without a retrieval requirement, treats recent computation as fresh data, or claims offline accuracy proves business impact.

Technical reference checked 2026-10-19: Feast point-in-time join documentation explains reconstructing feature state at historical timestamps. Availability-time handling, operational budgets, and model choices here are explicit exercise design decisions.

A short spoken walkthrough

Candidate: May recommendations fall back when features are too old?
Interviewer: Yes, use a safe non-personalized list.
Candidate: I will start with the simplest durable path and state the boundary before distributing it.
Interviewer: Your latency is excellent but the model quality falls. What do you change first?
Candidate: I inspect feature age, missingness, model/schema version and training-serving agreement. Adding replicas does not repair wrong inputs. I canary the model and transformation together with quality and latency guardrails, then roll back the versioned bundle if they regress. Eligibility remains an authoritative filter, independent of model scores.
